candidates.source_body_excerpt: Claire Lord sits alone in her living room surrounded by head-high boxes. The small space between her sofa and TV is the only bit of the flat not crowded by cubes of clutter. To answer the door she has to clamber over yet more plastic tubs filled to the brim with her worldly possessions. The 56-year-old is ready to move out of her flat in Rochdale ’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks. She’s been ready for weeks. Claire was one of 229 households told they had to leave by landowners Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) in October 2025. Since then, droves have been moving out of the blocks. Only an estimated 90 households are still left in Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank. RBH says this has been done for safety reasons. The tower blocks face an uncertain future, with the question of demolition or refurbishment still on the table after a decade of limbo. No matter the decision, it is understood all residents will have to move out whilst work is done - whether that work is to decorate or destroy. Claire is one of the latest to be exiting the estate, but it’s not a move she really wanted to do. When describing the day when RBH told her they'd found some new digs for her, she said she was ‘gutted’. The security, the views, proximity to healthcare professionals and the community are the things she cherishes most about her flat. Claire will be moving to a bungalow across the road, behind Lidl. “There has been a delay because the lady who lived in the bungalow hadn't done work on the place for some time,” Claire explained. “They’ve had to do painting and decorating, rewiring, putting new doors on and a fresh kitchen. “So they’ve been getting it ready for me. RBH told me about four months ago that I’d be moving and were waiting for the date. “Every time I’ve gone down they’ve come up with more work and more work to do. I’ve been down every week to ask. “It’s always the same story - ‘something is being done’. I’ve still not got a move-in date, I think I’ll be told about a move-in date in four weeks. “I do love living here. The security is good and there isn’t much chance of you getting burgled. “It’s close to the shops in the town centre, my mental health team is nearby and my GP is just down the road. “But my biggest fear of moving is losing that security. I’ve been here (in Mardyke block) for 12 years and I've never had any trouble, it’s a good community. “If I could stay I would. It’s not good for my mental health. I don’t know whether I’m coming or going. “Being stuck halfway is no good as I just don’t know. They’re just going to plonk a day on me.” Claire has credited RBH with supporting her through the transition. She has regular contact with housing officers, but that doesn’t mean the transition process has been easy for her. Like many of the tenants, she just wants to know what’s happening with the blocks. Claire added: “We’ve had so many rumours about what is happening. We’ve heard they’re bringing in migrants in; that three are staying up and four are coming down; then we’ve had that they’re all staying up; then we’ve had they’re all coming down and they’re building 250 houses. “Nothing is set in concrete and they won’t tell us. It’s all just rumours.” Her friend Christine Hartley, who has lived in the Tentercroft block for 14 years, hasn’t accepted any new accommodation from RBH. She is still waiting on a 'like for like replacement', which she admits isn’t really possible due to the size of her two-bed flat. The 67-year-old said:

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A woman whose breast cancer was discovered through a routine NHS screening appointment is urging others not to ignore their invitations after doctors found the disease before she noticed any symptoms. Sarah Hickman, 50, said she had no concerns about her health when she attended her first routine mammogram after receiving an NHS invitation. However, just one day later she was asked to attend the Breast Unit at Bolton NHS Foundation Trust for further investigations. Following additional imaging, an ultrasound and a biopsy, Sarah was diagnosed with a small breast cancer that had been detected at a very early stage. Recalling the experience, she said: “Mine was a textbook case. "Because I'd turned 50, I'd received my invitation for routine screening and went along without any concerns. "The next day I received a message asking me to come to Bolton for further tests. "It all happened very quickly, but throughout the process I felt completely reassured.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: John Doolan challenged rampant Accrington to push for the play-offs after they cruised to the biggest away win in their Football League history at toothless Rochdale. Josh Woods, Charlie Warren, Tyler Walton – with a brace – and substitute Alex Henderson all struck in a dominant 5-0 victory as Stanley made it nine games in a row unbeaten in all competitions. Remarkably, it was also their first away win since February but it took them up to ninth in League Two. Asked if the play-offs were a genuine incentive for Accy, boss Doolan – whose team finished 16th last term – said: “Yeah, it always has been for us. “We say to the players, you’re trying to progress and develop and be better than last year, and last year at one point, round about February, we were six points off the play-offs. “So to be sitting where we are now, one point off the play-offs, is credit to the players.” Doolan savoured the “outstanding” goals Accy scored as he urged them to build on what he felt was “probably” the best performance of his two-and-a-half-year reign. “A result like that just helps build momentum,” he said. “I think we’ve had that for the past eight, nine games now.

Tyler Walton notched a double as on-song Accrington extended their unbeaten run to nine games in all competitions with an emphatic 5-0 win at Rochdale.

The points were all but secured by half-time as John Doolan's side fired home three impressive strikes before the break on the way to their biggest victory since March 2025.

Dale were booed off after a fifth successive match without victory.

Stanley grabbed the lead in the 14th minute when Josh Woods guided in a low effort from 20 yards out after home goalkeeper Sam Waller passed the ball straight to him.

Walton then slipped a lovely pass through for Charlie Warren to lash a low strike in off the post from the edge of the box in the 38th minute.

Walton arced a stunning angled strike over Waller from just inside the box in first-half stoppage time.

The winger doubled his tally in the 51st minute when he knocked in the rebound after Joe Anderson's shot was saved by Waller.

Sub Alex Henderson sealed the rout in the 66th minute by finishing off a brilliant move from 10 yards out.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale council has raked in £2.88m from parking fines in the last three years. Data obtained from a Freedom of Information (FOI) request revealed that the local authority has generated just under £1m per year from 2023 to 2026. From a total of 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) issued for 2023, 2024 and 2025, the council gained £2.88m, with the highest earning year being 2025 with £990,256. The total value of PCNs was just over £5.6m, but the income is less due to people successfully challenging claims or costs of chasing fines. The town hall says all money generated from PCNs is then reinvested into the road network. This reinvestment could include fixing potholes, re-drawing on road markers or larger infrastructure projects. The local authority also pointed out PCNs are issued for safety reasons, such as making sure pavements have enough space for wheelchair users or to prevent blind spots at junctions. The FOI, submitted by the Local Democracy Reporting Service, also revealed the biggest hotspots in the borough where people get PCNs. Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central and Oldham Road Central were all the places with the highest number of PCNs distributed. Newgate: Number of PCNs – 790, total income: £54,920 Yorkshire St Central: Number of PCNs – 623, total income: £39,970

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill.

The incidents took place on October 13 and 14, with school crossing patrol Barry Jones having to move out of the way to avoid the vehicles, even though he was already standing in the road. The matter was reported to police, who used new powers under section 59 of the police reform act 2002, to seize the vehicles after collecting evidence, including witness statements. Cars and other vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols is a growing problem, with 137 fail to stops reported across Rochdale borough over the past five years. Body-worn cameras are now being used in hotspot areas to try to deter dangerous driving and support prosecutions where needed. Cllr Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways and facilities, said: “It beggars belief that somebody would see a school crossing patrol clearly standing in the middle of the road and continue to drive. Frankly I’m appalled. “We would like to thank GMP for their quick and decisive action and I think it’s a really good result.

The incidents took place on Tuesday, 13 and Wednesday, 14 October 2026, with school crossing patrol, Barry Jones, having to move out of the way to avoid the vehicles, a moped and a silver Skoda, even though he was already standing in the road. Fortunately, nobody was injured in the incident. The matter was reported to police, who used new powers under section 59 of the police reform act 2002, to seize the vehicles after collecting evidence, including witness statements. Cars and other vehicles failing to stop for school crossing patrols is a growing problem, with 137 fail to stops reported across Rochdale borough over the past 5 years. Body worn cameras are now being used in hotspot areas to try to deter dangerous driving and support prosecutions where needed. Councillor Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways and facilities, said: “It beggars belief that somebody would see a school crossing patrol clearly standing in the middle of the road and continue to drive. Frankly I’m appalled. “We would like to thank GMP for their quick and decisive action and I think it’s a really good result.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Chris Cheap has been appointed managing director of the development corporation overseeing Northern Gateway, a regeneration programme spanning Bury and Rochdale. He joins the Atom Valley Northern Gateway Mayoral Development Corporation after almost 23 years at property adviser Avison Young. His most recent role involved leading its UK transactional team, overseeing capital markets, leasing and development across the industrial, office and retail sectors. The corporation has been established to coordinate new homes, employment space and infrastructure at Northern Gateway, working with councils and other partners. The programme forms part of the wider Atom Valley Mayoral Development Zone, which stretches across Bury, Oldham and Rochdale. Mr Cheap said delivering the development would require cooperation between the public and private sectors. He said, “The MDC will play a pivotal role in this and I am pleased to bring my extensive real estate experience and leadership to the team.” One of Northern Gateway’s planned projects will improve road connections between the site and the M66 and M60. The work is intended to enable further development and complement capacity improvements at Simister Island.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A Rochdale woman who lost 12st 3lb has met double Olympic boxing champion Nicola Adams after reaching the semi-finals of Slimming World’s Woman of the Year competition. Vikki Gurney, 39, was one of 38 women to reach the national semi-finals, held at the organisation’s head office in Derbyshire. Members of her Cutgate group voted for her to represent them in the 2026 competition after she reduced her weight from 22st 1lb to 9st 12lb. Vikki said seeing a photograph of herself at a friend’s wedding prompted her to join the group. She said losing weight had helped her feel more confident about taking part in activities with her children. “For the first time, I found an eating plan that worked with real life. I never felt deprived, and I didn't have to give up the foods I loved.” Vikki said she changed how she prepared meals and found encouragement through weekly meetings with other members and consultant Alyson Hartley. “The support and encouragement I received each week gave me the confidence to keep going. candidates.source_body_excerpt: M6 Theatre Company has been awarded £73,500 from The National Lottery Heritage Fund to record its history and celebrate its 50th anniversary in 2027. The Rochdale company will create an oral history project, an interactive exhibition and a publicly accessible digital archive during a year-long programme. Founded in 1977, M6 specialises in touring theatre for children and young people. Its anniversary plans also include community outreach projects, a new youth theatre show, a community gala and a specially commissioned film and poem. Laura Rodwell, from M6 Theatre, said hundreds of local people would take part in the heritage activities. She said, “Hundreds of local people will participate in heritage activities and we will work with our communities to share and celebrate both M6’s journey over 50 years, and the journeys of our audiences, participants and theatre professionals past and present.” The project will collect stories and memories from people involved with the company over the past five decades. Helen Featherstone, director for England, North at The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said M6 had worked with more than 500,000 children and young people.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A court has ruled that Rochdale Council did not act unfairly in its decision not to pass ownership of Hopwood Hall to one of its descendants. Today marked the end of a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester after Hopwood DePree took legal action against the council which ended an exclusivity agreement to sell the historic Grade II-listed hall to him. Following the decision, Mr DePree said: “This is of course incredibly disappointing and a huge blow to our community, our supporters around the world, as well as the UK’s charitable heritage rescue groups in general. “However, please know that my team and I are already determining our legal options and next steps. “We will be watching closely to keep an eye on Rochdale Borough Council’s efforts to save Hopwood Hall for the community, and restore it to its former glory.” Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. READ MORE:Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026 Finalists Announced

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Police are hunting for a woman believed to have recently given birth on a Rochdale street after suspected human tissue was found nearby. Officers were called to reports of the discovery off Kingsway shortly before 9am on Thursday, triggering an investigation by Greater Manchester Police. Detectives said evidence recovered near the junction of Watkins Street and Charter Street indicated that a woman may have given birth in the vicinity. The force has appealed for information as concerns mount over the woman's wellbeing, cautioning that she may require immediate medical attention, according to The Mirror. Locating the woman is the police's "absolute priority" at this moment, as she may be in need of urgent medical attention, said Detective Inspector Daniel Daly, from GMP's Rochdale CID. Anyone who may have spotted a woman in distress, or who holds any information relating to the incident, is being urged to get in touch with Greater Manchester Police. "Since receiving the report earlier today, we have been carrying out a number of lines of enquiry but our priority to find the woman and make sure she is safe and well," Detective Daly said. "She may be in need of urgent medical attention, and she is our absolute priority at the moment - that is why we are asking anyone with information to contact us. "Anyone with information, or who may have seen a woman in distress, is asked to call us on 101 and quote incident number 684 of 22/10/2026. Information can also be reported online or by using our LiveChat service at www.gmp.police.uk. Alternatively, contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111. "We would ask that people don't speculate on the circumstances of this discovery as it hinders our investigation and is upsetting for those involved."

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Campaigners calling for better diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis have met with an MP to help improve workplaces for women suffering with the debilitating condition. Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell invited Dr Anita Sharma, GP and chair and founder of the Endometriosis Awareness North Charity, with other local campaigners to Westminster for an event focused on the importance of improving workplaces for women with endometriosis. It is an issue Mrs Blundell has championed since her election. Endometriosis is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, causing inflammation, pain, scarring, and fertility issues. There is currently an average nine-year waiting list for diagnosis and treatment. Campaigners say too many employers are without the knowledge, means or will to ensure that women with this condition are supported, protected and enabled to progress. Mrs Blundell said: “I was very pleased to welcome Anita, Laura, Courtney, Lucy and Lorna to Parliament to participate in a moment of real reflection for MPs and their constituents from across the country and all political parties. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans for a town centre takeaway have been refused on health grounds because there are already too many-fast-food restaurants in the area. Sheeraz Ahmed applied to Rochdale Council for permission to turn a shop into a fast-food takeaway at 159 Yorkshire Street, Rochdale. The site had most recently been home to Ria Money Transfer. In documents submitted with the application, Building Design Services said: “The proposal seeks to introduce a takeaway business operating primarily as a collection and delivery-based food establishment serving a variety of hot food products, including burgers, fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs, desserts, waffles and milkshakes. “The proposed development would involve internal alterations to facilitate the operation of the takeaway, including the provision of customer serving areas, food preparation spaces, cooking facilities, staff welfare facilities and ancillary storage areas. “The premises would operate as a takeaway only establishment with no internal seating proposed for customers.” The proposed opening hours were from 11am to 11pm and the takeaway would have created four jobs. But the application raised concerns about people’s eating habits and the number of fast-food restaurants and takeaways already in the area. A planning officer’s report referenced the council’s Public Health officer, who noted: “The planning application will increase the availability of food high in fat, salt, and sugar, and a health impact assessment has not been carried out, and as such I request that the development is not approved.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Renovating Rochdale’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks would force residents out of their homes for more than a decade, housing chiefs have said. While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale is celebrating a blooming brilliant victory after striking gold at this year’s Britain in Bloom awards and being crowned the overall winner of the Town Centres and City Centres category. Rochdale was placed ahead of Floral Godalming (Southeast), Shaftesbury in Bloom (South) and Sidcup Partners Limited (London). Rochdale in Bloom has a proud competition record, securing gold in 2018, being named Best Small City in 2022 and winning gold again for Rochdale town centre in 2024. This year’s category win keeps the title in the borough after Middleton town centre took the top prize last year. Rochdale has undergone significant regeneration in recent years. The Grade I-listed Rochdale Town Hall has been expertly restored, complemented by the creation of the new Town Hall Square and the transformation of the Broadfield Park slopes. Supported by a multi-million-pound National Lottery Heritage Fund grant, have made this historic quarter the envy of many. Judges praised Rochdale town centre’s vibrant displays from Bowlee Garden Nursery, recycling initiatives and exceptional cleanliness, as well as the pride, teamwork and dedication of everyone involved. They also recognised the commitment to local biodiversity and strong partnerships, with Rochdale exceeding the gold standard in horticulture, environmental responsibility and community participation. Rochdale’s historic Baillie Street Quarter and striking murals, created through the 2025 Rochdale Common Walls Festival, strengthened the town centre’s entry by showcasing its culture and civic pride. Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader and cabinet member for climate change and environment at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “What another outstanding achievement for our borough. Last year, Middleton town centre achieved gold and was overall category winner and now Rochdale town centre is back as a worthy winner once again championing our borough for 2026.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale Town Hall’s Martlet Kitchen has picked up the Trip Advisor Travellers’ Choice Award 2026, placing it among the top-rated restaurants in the world on the popular review site. The award honours businesses which consistently receive great reviews, with their scores placing them in the top 10 per cent of all establishments registered on the popular review site. With millions of businesses from around the globe listed on the site, the award is a huge accolade for the Martlet Kitchen, which recently celebrated its second birthday. It’s not the first time the restaurant, which specialises in traditional, high-quality British food, has been lauded. In his food column for The Guardian, legendary food critic Jay Rayner, described the Martlet Kitchen as a ‘victory of professionalism, good sense and, most of all, great taste and skill’ when he visited shortly after its opening in 2024. The Martlet Kitchen is helmed by multi award winning chef, Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College before working at acclaimed establishments including Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden, both of which boast 2 AA rosettes. Rooted in the community, its food and drink is sourced from the local area, including Milnrow’s Jacksons Farm, Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill and Grandpa Greene’s in Oldham. “This award is great news and we’re aiming for more accolades in the future. It’s about good old fashioned British grub, cooked to perfection, using top quality local ingredients, coupled with excellent service.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: The battle for Hopwood Hall returns to the courtroom today with ownership of the historic manor house at stake. Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council begin a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester later over Mr DePree’s bid to restore his ancestral home. Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. The legal action initiated by Mr DePree was launched after he spent seven years working with the council to carry out vital repairs on the dilapidated site with a view to purchasing it. In November, 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with Mr DePree, and said it would explore other options because no “commercially viable” business model had been presented. READ MORE: Four arrests and £1m drugs seizure in Rochdale Mr DePree’s case is that the council went back on his option to purchase Hopwood Hall upon planning permission being granted in 2022. His claim is that the agreement triggers have been satisfied and the council must proceed with the ownership transfer.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: The Martlet Kitchen at Rochdale Town Hall has won a Tripadvisor Travellers’ Choice Award for 2026 following reviews from its customers. The award recognises businesses which consistently receive positive reviews, placing them among the top 10 per cent of listings on the review site. The restaurant opened in 2024 and is led by chef Darren Parkinson, who trained at Hopwood Hall College. He previously worked at Shibden Mill Inn in Halifax and the Fleece Inn in Ripponden. Its suppliers include Jacksons Farm in Milnrow, Defiance Distillery at Spotland Mill and Grandpa Greene’s in Oldham. Darren said: “This award is great news and we’re aiming for more accolades in the future. It’s about good old fashioned British grub, cooked to perfection, using top quality local ingredients, coupled with excellent service.” Restaurant manager Sarah Crabtree said the team regularly changes the menu while retaining dishes such as fish and chips. She said: “Everyone who works here takes huge pride in their job, so the experience for the customers is really consistent.” The Martlet Kitchen serves breakfast and lunch, with a grill club on Fridays and fine dining on Saturday evenings. It has also introduced private dining in the Mayor’s reception room at the Grade I listed town hall.
